title: Open for Extension, Closed for Modification

content.title: Open for Extension, Closed for Modification

blocks.content: The SOLID Principles module introduced the Open/Closed Principle briefly, open for extension, closed for modification.
This lesson comes back to it with the concrete extensibility techniques from the previous topic already in hand, and looks at what actually applying it looks like in real code.
By the end, you should be able to recognize a violation, fix it with a concrete technique, and know when strict adherence is not worth the ceremony.
A module is open for extension when new behavior can be added, and closed for modification when adding that behavior never requires editing its existing, already tested code.
1. A Quick Recap of the Principle
blocks.text: 1. A Quick Recap of the Principle

blocks.content: Open for extension means new capability can always be added.
Closed for modification means adding that capability never requires reopening the class that already works.
Both halves sound abstract until you see them fail independently, so it helps to look at each in isolation first.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512510527-599835362.png
blocks.alt: A core class stays closed while a new subclass is added alongside it for extension, contrasted with directly editing the existing code

blocks.content: Why both halves matter together
Extension alone is easy, you can always add new capability by editing existing code. The principle is only interesting because it insists on extension without modification.

["Extension without closure is just ordinary code changes, nothing special.","Closure without extension would mean a class that can never gain new capability at all, which is too rigid to be useful.","The principle asks for both together, new capability, zero edits to what already works."]
items: Extension without closure is just ordinary code changes, nothing special.
Closure without extension would mean a class that can never gain new capability at all, which is too rigid to be useful.
The principle asks for both together, new capability, zero edits to what already works.

blocks.content: 2. Why Modifying Existing Tested Code Is Risky
blocks.text: 2. Why Modifying Existing Tested Code Is Risky

blocks.content: This is the actual reason the principle exists, not an abstract preference for clean code.
It is worth spending a moment on the mechanics of exactly how a small edit turns into a large incident.
Code that already works has, by definition, already been tested and trusted by whoever depends on it.
Every edit to that code reopens all of that trust at once, even if the edit is meant to only affect one narrow case.
This effect has a name worth remembering.
The blast radius problem
A one line change inside a shared method can silently affect every single caller of that method, not just the one you had in mind.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512515083-434859079.png
blocks.alt: A single one line edit inside a shared method reaching every caller of that method at once

blocks.title: A real world near miss
blocks.text: An engineer adds a new discount type by inserting a branch near the top of a pricing method. The new branch subtly changes float rounding for an unrelated case two branches down, and a customer is undercharged for weeks before anyone notices.

blocks.title: The core insight
blocks.content: Adding new code next to existing code cannot break the existing code. Editing existing code always can, no matter how careful the edit looks.
3. Abstract Base Classes as an Extension Mechanism
blocks.text: 3. Abstract Base Classes as an Extension Mechanism

blocks.content: This is the most direct, language level way to open a design for extension.
One classic way to satisfy Open/Closed is defining an abstract base class that captures the shared shape, letting each variant extend it independently.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512516839-71591603.png
blocks.alt: An abstract Discount base class with existing Percentage and Flat subclasses, and a new Seasonal subclass added later without touching the base or its siblings

blocks.content: A new discount type becomes a new subclass. Discount itself, and every existing subclass, stays completely untouched.
That untouched guarantee is the entire point, not a side effect.
It is also what makes independent testing of PercentageDiscount and FlatDiscount possible without any shared setup.
4. Strategy Pattern as an Extension Mechanism
blocks.text: 4. Strategy Pattern as an Extension Mechanism

blocks.content: If Abstract Base Classes are the foundation, Strategy is the most common practical shape built on top of it.
Strategy is really the same idea applied specifically to swappable algorithms or behaviors chosen at runtime.
Instead of a class inheriting a fixed behavior, it holds a reference to a strategy object and delegates to it.
PriceCalculator never changes no matter how many discount strategies exist, it only ever calls the shared apply method.
This should feel familiar, it is the same shape covered in the Strategy pattern lesson earlier in this course.
Seeing it reappear here should reinforce just how broadly this one pattern applies.
5. Decorator Pattern as an Extension Mechanism
blocks.text: 5. Decorator Pattern as an Extension Mechanism

blocks.content: Strategy handles picking one behavior. Decorator handles layering several behaviors together.
Decorator wraps an existing object with new behavior layered around it, without changing the object being wrapped.
This is useful when new behavior needs to combine with existing behavior rather than replace it entirely, like stacking multiple discounts.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512518569-767984834.png
blocks.alt: A base discount wrapped by a loyalty decorator and then a seasonal decorator, layering behavior to produce a final stacked price

blocks.content: Neither PercentageDiscount nor the base Discount class needed a single edit to support this new stacked behavior.
Stacking a third or fourth discount later follows the exact same wrapping approach.
Each new layer is its own small, independently testable class.
6. A Worked Discount Calculation Refactor
Seeing the full before and after in one place ties every technique from this lesson together.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783496818102-573054909.png
blocks.alt: A stable core with three new behaviors added alongside it, none of them requiring the core itself to be modified

blocks.content: Picture a discount system that started as a single if-else chain, the same rigid shape covered in the previous lesson.
After applying the Discount abstraction and Strategy pattern shown earlier, a brand new seasonal discount can be added as follows.
Notice how little new surface area this change actually touches.
One new file, one new class, and nothing else in the codebase needs to know it exists until it is wired in.
PriceCalculator, Discount, PercentageDiscount, and FlatDiscount are all exactly as they were before this addition.
That is the entire promise of Open/Closed, made concrete in one small example.

6.5. Recognizing a Violation in Code Review
blocks.text: 6.5. Recognizing a Violation in Code Review

blocks.content: Once you know what to look for, Open/Closed violations become easy to spot in a pull request.
The telltale diff shape
A diff that adds a new else-if or case branch to an existing method, rather than adding a new file, is almost always a violation waiting to be refactored.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512520168-318490807.png
blocks.alt: An if-else chain handling a type field growing a third and fourth branch over time, the pattern a reviewer should flag

blocks.content: ["A new branch added to an existing switch or if-else chain handling a type field.","A new parameter added to a shared function purely to change its behavior for one caller.","A comment reading something like special case for the new client, inserted into shared logic."]
items: A new branch added to an existing switch or if-else chain handling a type field.
A new parameter added to a shared function purely to change its behavior for one caller.
A comment reading something like special case for the new client, inserted into shared logic.

blocks.content: None of this means every new branch is wrong, a one off script or a class with only ever two cases is often fine as is.
Context always matters more than a rigid rule applied without thinking.
The signal worth watching for is the same branch growing a third, fourth, and fifth case over time, that pattern is what justifies the refactor.

blocks.title: A review habit worth building
blocks.content: Ask whether this pull request could have been a new file instead of an edit to an existing one. If the answer is clearly yes and the class already has this pattern of repeated edits, flag it.
7. When Strict Adherence Is Not Worth It
blocks.text: 7. When Strict Adherence Is Not Worth It

blocks.content: Every technique shown so far adds a small amount of structure. That structure needs to earn its place.
This principle, like every principle in this course, has a cost, and that cost is not always worth paying.
Not every piece of logic deserves an abstraction built around future flexibility.
A genuinely small, stable case

A tax calculation with exactly two fixed brackets that a government sets once a year, and essentially never changes structurally, does not need an abstraction built in preparation for a third bracket type that may never come.

{"pros":["New behavior ships without risking already tested code","Code review for a new feature stays scoped to just that feature","Independent behaviors can be tested completely in isolation"],"cons":["Extra interface or abstract class for behavior that may only ever have one implementation","Slightly more files and indirection to navigate for a simple case","Can encourage speculative extension points nobody ends up needing"]}

blocks.title: A practical rule
blocks.content: Apply Open/Closed once you have already seen a second variant, or you are confident a second variant is genuinely coming soon. Otherwise, a direct implementation you can refactor later is completely reasonable.
Refactoring later is not a failure
blocks.text: Refactoring later is not a failure

blocks.content: Starting with a simple if-else and refactoring to Strategy once a third case appears is a perfectly normal, healthy path, not a sign of a bad initial design.

{"headers":["Signal","Suggests"],"rows":[["One or two stable cases, unlikely to grow","A direct implementation is fine, skip the abstraction for now"],["A third case just appeared","Good moment to extract an extension point"],["Cases are added every release cycle","The abstraction should already exist"]]}
7.5. Combining Techniques in Practice
Real systems rarely use just one technique in isolation, they usually combine a few of the ones covered in this lesson.
A layered example

A billing system might use Abstract Base Classes for the core discount contract, Strategy to pick one discount for a given order, and Decorator to stack a loyalty bonus on top of whichever discount was chosen.
Every piece here, PercentageDiscount, LoyaltyDiscountDecorator, and PriceCalculator, was written once and never touched again as new combinations appeared.
That is a strong signal the abstraction boundaries were drawn in the right place.
This composability is the real, compounding payoff of applying Open/Closed consistently across a codebase rather than in one isolated spot.
8. Closing This Module
This is the last topic in Dependency Management and Extensibility, so it is worth stepping back before moving on.
This closes out the Dependency Management and Extensibility module.
Take a moment to notice how naturally the three lessons built on each other.
Three lessons, one underlying theme, worth restating plainly.

["Inversion of Control, decide who really controls a dependency or a decision.","Designing for Extensibility, notice real repeated variation and build a seam for exactly that.","Open and Closed, once that seam exists, grow behavior alongside it instead of editing it."]
items: Inversion of Control, decide who really controls a dependency or a decision.
Designing for Extensibility, notice real repeated variation and build a seam for exactly that.
Open and Closed, once that seam exists, grow behavior alongside it instead of editing it.

blocks.content: Across Inversion of Control, Designing for Extensibility, and Open/Closed here, one thread runs through all three, control and change should live at seams you choose deliberately, not scattered wherever a class happens to need something.

None of these ideas ask you to predict the future perfectly. They ask you to notice real, repeated variation when it shows up, and to respond to it with a specific, well understood technique rather than either rigid code or speculative abstraction.
That balance, structure exactly where it earns its keep and simplicity everywhere else, is the actual skill this module has been building toward.
Carry it forward into every design decision from here, including the ones covered in later modules of this course.
When in doubt, prefer the simpler version today, and refactor once real variation actually shows up.
That single habit will serve you well long after the specific patterns in this lesson are second nature.
Good design is a practice, not a checklist, and it gets sharper the more you apply it deliberately.
Closed for modification is a promise to your future self and your team. Keep that promise only where it is actually worth keeping.
